checks.original: On July 16, 1969, a 363-foot Saturn V rocket lifted Apollo 11 from Kennedy Space Center.
The crew was Neil Armstrong, Michael Collins, and Edwin Aldrin Jr.
Armstrong and Aldrin descended in the Lunar Module Eagle while Collins orbited in the Command Module Columbia.
They landed at the Sea of Tranquility on July 20, 1969, becoming the first humans on the Moon.
Armstrong stepped out first, saying his famous words about a step and a leap.
An estimated 650 million people watched the historic moment live on television.
They left a plaque reading: Here men from Earth first set foot on the Moon, July 1969.
Apollo 11 splashed down in the Pacific on July 24, 1969, completing the first lunar landing mission.

facts.text: Apollo 11 launched from Cape Kennedy on July 16, 1969, carrying three astronauts into Earth orbit.
facts.quote: Apollo 11 launched from Cape Kennedy on July 16, 1969, carrying Commander Neil Armstrong, Command Module Pilot Michael Collins and Lunar Module Pilot Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin into an initial Earth-orbit of 114 by 116 miles.

facts.text: Neil Armstrong took his famous first step on the Moon on July 20, 1969, watched by an estimated 650 million people.
facts.quote: An estimated 650 million people watched Armstrong’s televised image and heard his voice describe the event as he took “…one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind” on July 20, 1969.

facts.text: Apollo 11 splashed down in the Pacific Ocean on July 24, 1969, 13 miles from the recovery ship USS Hornet.
facts.quote: After a flight of 195 hours, 18 minutes, 35 seconds – about 36 minutes longer than planned – Apollo 11 splashed down in the Pacific Ocean, 13 miles from the recovery ship USS Hornet.

facts.text: The landing point was changed by about 250 miles due to bad weather in the target area.
facts.quote: Because of bad weather in the target area, the landing point was changed by about 250 miles.

facts.text: Apollo 11 landed at 13 degrees, 19 minutes north latitude and 169 degrees, nine minutes west longitude on July 24, 1969.
facts.quote: Apollo 11 landed 13 degrees, 19 minutes north latitude and 169 degrees, nine minutes west longitude July 24, 1969.

facts.text: Neil Armstrong was the first person to walk on the Moon, about six-and-a-half hours after landing.
facts.quote: About six-and-a-half hours later, Armstrong became the first person to walk on the moon.

facts.text: Armstrong's famous quote was "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."
facts.quote: As he took his first step, Armstrong famously said, "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."

facts.text: A plaque left on the Moon read "Here men from the planet Earth first set foot on the moon—July 1969 A.D.—We came in peace for all mankind."
facts.quote: Among the items left on the surface of the moon was a plaque that read: "Here men from the planet Earth first set foot on the moon—July 1969 A.D.—We came in peace for all mankind."

facts.text: Apollo 11 astronauts Neil A. Armstrong, Michael Collins, and Edwin E. Aldrin Jr. launched on July 16, 1969 at 9:32 a.m. EDT from Kennedy Space Center's Launch Complex 39A.
facts.quote: The Apollo 11 Saturn V lifts off with astronauts Neil A. Armstrong, Michael Collins and Edwin E. Aldrin Jr. at 9:32 a.m. EDT July 16, 1969, from Kennedy Space Center's Launch Complex 39A.

facts.text: Apollo 11 was the first mission to achieve a lunar landing.
facts.quote: The American flag heralds the flight of Apollo 11, the first lunar landing mission.

facts.text: Vice President Spiro Agnew and former President Lyndon Johnson viewed the Apollo 11 liftoff from the Kennedy Space Center VIP viewing site.
facts.quote: Vice President Spiro Agnew (right center) and former President Lyndon Johnson (left center) view the liftoff of Apollo 11 from the stands located at the Kennedy Space Center VIP viewing site.

facts.text: Mission officials relaxed in the Launch Control Center after the successful Apollo 11 liftoff.
facts.quote: Apollo 11 mission officials relax in the Launch Control Center following the successful liftoff of Apollo 11.

facts.text: Apollo 11 launch was monitored from Mission Control with men using headsets at control desks.
facts.quote: Men with headsets at control desk in Mission Control

facts.text: Apollo 11 was the first crewed mission to land on the Moon.
facts.quote: It fulfilled a national goal set by President John F. Kennedy in May 1961, who had challenged the United States to land a man on the Moon and return him safely before the end of the decade.

facts.text: The mission fulfilled a goal set by President John F. Kennedy in 1961.
facts.quote: It fulfilled a national goal set by President John F. Kennedy in May 1961, who had challenged the United States to land a man on the Moon and return him safely before the end of the decade.

facts.text: The Soviet Luna 15 probe crashed on the Moon while Armstrong and Aldrin were on the surface.
facts.quote: the Soviet Union, despite early leads in spaceflight, was unable to match the Saturn V rocket, and its uncrewed lunar probe Luna 15 crashed on the Moon on July 21, while Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin were still on the lunar surface.

facts.text: The crew visited multiple countries including West Berlin and Belgrade after the mission.
facts.quote: In London the astronauts went to Buckingham Palace, where they were greeted by Queen Elizabeth II. When they went to West Berlin, they were given a tour of the Berlin Wall by the city's mayor. In Belgrade they were greeted by a crowd of between 400,000 and 500,000 people...

facts.text: Apollo 11 followed the Mercury and Gemini programs.
facts.quote: The program overcame a severe setback with the fatal Apollo 1 launchpad fire in January 1967 and drew on technologies developed through the preceding Mercury and Gemini programs.

facts.text: Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space and to orbit Earth on April 12, 1961.
facts.quote: The Soviets took the lead on April 12, 1961, when cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space and the first to orbit the Earth.

facts.text: Apollo 11 was the first mission to land humans on the Moon on July 20, 1969.
facts.quote: The first moon landing was Apollo 11. It landed on July 20, 1969.

facts.text: The Apollo 11 crew consisted of Neil Armstrong, Michael Collins, and Buzz Aldrin.
facts.quote: The crew of Apollo 11 was Neil Armstrong, Michael Collins and Buzz Aldrin.

facts.text: Neil Armstrong was the first person to walk on the Moon; Buzz Aldrin also walked on the Moon while Michael Collins orbited above.
facts.quote: Armstrong and Aldrin walked on the moon. Collins stayed in orbit around the moon. Neil Armstrong was the first person to walk on the moon.

facts.text: The Saturn V rocket, standing 36 stories tall, was used to launch Apollo 11 to the Moon.
facts.quote: The Saturn V was as tall as a 36-story building.

facts.text: Apollo 11 launched from Kennedy Space Center's Launch Complex 39A on July 16, 1969 at 9:32 a.m. EDT.
facts.quote: The Apollo 11 Saturn V lifts off with astronauts Neil A. Armstrong, Michael Collins and Edwin E. Aldrin Jr. at 9:32 a.m. EDT July 16, 1969, from Kennedy’s Launch Complex 39A.

facts.text: Apollo 13, though intended to land on the Moon, suffered a malfunction and did not land, instead orbiting the Moon before returning safely to Earth.
facts.quote: Apollo 13 was going to land on the moon. On the way there, the spacecraft had a problem. NASA had to figure out how to bring the astronauts home safely. They flew all the way around the moon before returning home.

facts.text: Cape Canaveral was renamed to Cape Kennedy on November 29, 1963, following President Kennedy's death.
facts.quote: President Lyndon B. Johnson, issued Executive Order 11129 renaming both NASA's Merritt Island Launch Operations Center and "the facilities of Station No. 1 of the Atlantic Missile Range" (a reference to the Cape Canaveral Missile Test Annex) as the "John F. Kennedy Space Center". He had also convinced then-Florida Governor C. Farris Bryant (D-Florida) to change the name of Cape Canaveral to Cape Kennedy.

facts.text: The Air Force launch site at Cape Canaveral was named Cape Kennedy Air Force Station during the Apollo program.
facts.quote: a general order renaming the Air Force launch site Cape Kennedy Air Force Station. This name was used through the Project Gemini and early Apollo program.

facts.text: Cape Canaveral was known as Cape Canaveral Launch Area upon its foundation in 1949 but renamed to LRPG Launching Area in 1950.
facts.quote: Cape Canaveral was known as Cape Canaveral Launch Area upon its foundation in 1949, but renamed to LRPG Launching Area in 1950.

facts.text: Cape Canaveral was known as Cape Canaveral Auxiliary Air Force Base from 1951 to 1955 and Cape Canaveral Missile Test Annex from 1955 to 1964.
facts.quote: It was known as Cape Canaveral Auxiliary Air Force Base from 1951 to 1955, and Cape Canaveral Missile Test Annex from 1955 to 1964.

facts.text: Cape Canaveral was known as Cape Kennedy Air Force Station from 1964 to 1974.
facts.quote: The facility was known as Cape Kennedy Air Force Station from 1964 to 1974,

facts.text: Cape Canaveral Space Force Station was renamed in December 2020.
facts.quote: The facility was renamed "Cape Canaveral Space Force Station" in December 2020.

facts.text: Apollo 11 was the United States' first lunar landing mission.
facts.quote: Apollo 11 was the United States’ first lunar landing mission.

facts.text: Saturn V rocket was 363 feet tall and launched from Pad A, Launch Complex 39 at Kennedy Space Center.
facts.quote: the huge, 363-feet tall Saturn V rocket launches on the Apollo 11 mission from Pad A, Launch Complex 39, Kennedy Space Center

facts.text: Apollo 11 launched on July 16, 1969 at 9:32 a.m. EDT.
facts.quote: On July 16, 1969, the huge, 363-feet tall Saturn V rocket launches on the Apollo 11 mission from Pad A, Launch Complex 39, Kennedy Space Center, at 9:32 a.m. EDT.

facts.text: Crew members were Neil A. Armstrong (commander), Michael Collins (command module pilot), and Edwin E. Aldrin Jr. (lunar module pilot).
facts.quote: Onboard the Apollo 11 spacecraft are astronauts Neil A. Armstrong, commander; Michael Collins, command module pilot; and Edwin E. Aldrin Jr., lunar module pilot.

facts.text: Neil Armstrong and Edwin Aldrin descended to the moon in the Lunar Module Eagle while Michael Collins orbited in the Command Module Columbia.
facts.quote: While astronauts Armstrong and Aldrin descended in the Lunar Module “Eagle” to explore the Sea of Tranquility region of the moon, astronaut Collins remained with the Command and Service Modules “Columbia” in lunar orbit.

facts.text: The landing site was the Sea of Tranquility on the moon.
facts.quote: While astronauts Armstrong and Aldrin descended in the Lunar Module “Eagle” to explore the Sea of Tranquility region of the moon, astronaut Collins remained with the Command and Service Modules “Columbia” in lunar orbit.

facts.text: Apollo 11 astronaut Neil Armstrong first stepped onto the Moon on July 20, 1969.
facts.quote: That's one small step for man, one giant leap for all mankind.

facts.text: Neil Armstrong's first step onto the Moon was watched by nearly 600 million people worldwide.
facts.quote: When Armstrong took those first few steps away from Eagle, nearly 600 million people watched.

facts.text: The Moon landing was the most watched event in television history.
facts.quote: The Moon landing was the most watched event in television history;

facts.text: President Nixon planned to proclaim July 20 a holiday called Moon Day so Americans could watch the astronauts' activity.
facts.quote: After a successful Translunar Injection, Nixon would proclaim July 20 a holiday—Moon Day—

facts.text: President Nixon would call the astronauts the day before their liftoff, while the first lady would call the astronauts' wives.
facts.quote: The President would call the astronauts the day before their liftoff, while the first lady would call the astronauts' wives.

facts.text: Once Armstrong and Aldrin were safely on the lunar surface, President Nixon made the world's first 'interplanetary' congratulatory telephone call.
facts.quote: Once Armstrong and Aldrin were safely on the surface, the President would make the world's first "interplanetary" congratulatory telephone call
